blocks.title: <ico-recycle></ico-recycle> RECAP · from C1
blocks.intro: Before you start at the Grand Hotel: five coded phrases from the end of C1. Match each one with what it usually means.

blocks.title: <ico-book></ico-book> THE RIGHT WORD
blocks.intro: At C2, nearly everything you say is correct. The question is no longer «is it right?» but «is it the word I mean?» Near-synonyms state the same fact and pass different judgments. Five steps on how a single word carries an opinion.

vocab.sp: the feeling a word carries, beyond its meaning
a soft word for a hard fact
expressed with less force than the facts deserve
to ask careful questions to find out more
a small printed booklet that advertises a place
a better room or seat than the one you paid for
to have a view of the inner yard
to choose to ignore the difference

blocks.note: How it works: compare , flashcards , listening , gap-fill , memory and a dialogue. From here on, every option is grammatical. You are choosing the one that fits.

parts.html: 1 · ONE FACT, THREE ATTITUDES — approving, neutral, critical

items.en: She is determined.
items.sp: She doesn't give up, and I admire it.

items.en: She is stubborn.
items.sp: She doesn't give up, and I wish she would.

items.en: She is pig-headed.
items.sp: The same, and I have lost patience.

items.en: The hotel is affordable. It is inexpensive. It is cheap.
items.sp: Good value · a neutral fact · possibly poor quality.

parts.html: 2 · REPORTING VERBS CARRY A VERDICT — the verb tells us what the speaker believes

items.en: The brochure said the room was quiet.
items.sp: Neutral: I pass it on.

items.en: The brochure claimed the room was quiet.
items.sp: I doubt it.

items.en: The manager admitted the room was noisy.
items.sp: It is true, and it was a fault.

items.en: The manager conceded that the view was limited.
items.sp: It is true, and he accepted it unwillingly.

parts.html: 3 · GRADABLE AND ABSOLUTE — each kind takes its own modifiers

items: fairly · rather · somewhat · very + tired, warm, good
absolutely · utterly · completely + exhausted, boiling, superb

items.en: I was very tired. I was absolutely exhausted.
items.sp: Tired has degrees; exhausted is already the top of the scale.

items.en: The room is rather warm.
items.sp: Rather + a quality you would prefer to be otherwise: a polite complaint.

items.en: The plan is utterly ridiculous.
items.sp: Utterly + an extreme adjective, usually a negative one.

parts.html: 4 · QUITE — one word, two directions

items.en: The food was quite good.
items.sp: With a gradable adjective. In American English: very good. In British English: fairly good, less than you hoped.

items.en: You are quite right. It is quite impossible.
items.sp: With an absolute adjective: completely. The same on both sides of the Atlantic.

parts.html: 5 · STANCE ADVERBS — one word at the front tells us how to take the rest

items.en: Arguably, it is the best room in the hotel.
items.sp: A case can be made. I am not insisting.

items.en: Presumably, the view was better before the tower was built.
items.sp: I suppose so; I have not checked.

items.en: Ostensibly, the upgrade was a gift.
items.sp: That is the official story. I suspect another one.

items.en: Admittedly, the bed is comfortable.
items.sp: I concede this point, against my own argument.

parts.html: CALQUE ALERT — four Spanish-shaped habits that survive at C2

items.en: The breakfast was absolutely delicious.
items.sp: Delicious and perfect are absolute: not «very delicious», not «very perfect».

items.en: I intend to stay for a week.
items.sp: To pretend is to act as if something were true. For a plan, use intend.

items.en: Eventually, they fixed the heating.
items.sp: Eventually = in the end, after a long time. It never means «possibly».

items.en: The manager was very sympathetic when I complained.
items.sp: Sympathetic = understanding of someone's trouble. For a pleasant person, say nice, friendly or likeable.

blocks.title: <ico-star></ico-star> THE RIGHT WORD
blocks.intro: The Grand Hotel is hosting a three-day summit of writers, academics, a comedian and a critic, and you are working the concierge desk with Julian. The first note of the weekend arrives from room 412. Sol, the novelist, describes her room in one word: «adequate». Julian reads it twice. «From a novelist, that is a complaint. Find out what kind.»

cast.sp: a novelist who chooses every word
at the concierge desk, listening closely

blocks.title: ADMITTED vs CLAIMED
blocks.intro: One verb is different. Everything the speaker believes about the room changes with it.

pair.a: She admitted the room was noisy.
pair.b: She claimed the room was noisy.

items.q: In which sentence does the speaker accept that the room really was noisy?
In which sentence does the speaker doubt it?
In A, who is "she" most likely to be?
options: A guest who wants a refund

items.q: Which is the natural partner for "chance"?
Which sentence would the hotel print in its own brochure?

blocks.title: THREE WORDS, ONE FACT · tap to flip
blocks.intro: Each card has three words for the same fact, from approving to critical. Before you flip, decide which one you would want said about you.

cards.back: approving · neutral · critical — «a slim figure», «thin walls», «he looks skinny»
approving · critical · insulting — the same refusal to give up
neutral · I doubt it · it's true and it was a fault
good value · neutral · maybe poor quality
approving · neutral · critical — all three spend little

blocks.title: AUDIO 1 · THE NOTE
blocks.desc: Julian goes up to room 412 and you go with him. Sol never raises her voice and never says what she wants. Listen to her adjectives, her adverbs and one verb.

options: A room with a real river view

questions.q: Why does she say the brochure "claimed" a view of the river?
options: She is quoting the brochure word for word
She doubts that the statement is true
She wants to praise the brochure

questions.q: What does "a somewhat ambitious description" tell us?
options: The description is long and detailed
The description promises more than the room delivers
No: she is dissatisfied, but courteous and rather amused
Yes: she is furious and wants to leave
No: she is perfectly happy with the room

speaking.prompt: Translate Sol into plain English. Say what she means by: 'rather warm', 'quite talkative' and 'a somewhat ambitious description'.
speaking.starter: When she says 'rather warm', she means… By 'quite talkative', she means… 'A somewhat ambitious description' means…

transcript.html: Good afternoon. Room four twelve, I believe. I'm Julian, from the concierge desk. I received your note.
Ah. Yes. I do hope it wasn't taken as a complaint.
You described the room as "adequate."
It is adequate. It has a bed, a desk and a door. I have written novels in worse.
And in better, I imagine. May I ask about the temperature?
Rather warm. Not unpleasant, exactly. One feels gently cooked.
I see. And the noise?
The room is not noisy. The elevator next to it, however, is quite talkative. It converses with itself until about two in the morning.
And the view? The brochure mentions a view of the river.

The brochure claimed a view of the river. I would call that a somewhat ambitious description. If I stand on the desk and lean to the left, there is, admittedly, a suggestion of water. Presumably the river.
Presumably.

Please don't misunderstand me. Your staff have been utterly charming, and the breakfast is absolutely superb. I am not an unreasonable woman. I simply came here to finish a chapter, and the chapter requires silence and, ideally, a temperature at which a person can think.
Then, if I may translate: you would like a cooler, quieter room, and the river is optional.
The river is entirely optional. You have understood me perfectly. How refreshing.
We have a room on the sixth floor, at the back. It overlooks the courtyard, which is not much to look at. But it is silent, and the windows open.
A window that opens. Now that is a luxury. Is it more expensive?
Ostensibly, yes. I think we can overlook the difference.
Julian, that is the most elegant sentence I have heard all week. I shall put you in the book.
As a hero, I hope.
As a concierge. It is higher praise.

blocks.title: WHICH ONE FITS?
blocks.intro: All three options are correct English. Read the whole sentence: the context tells you the attitude, the degree or the stance.

items.q: I'm not criticizing her. I admire how ___ she is: she never gives up.
He refuses to listen to anyone, and it has cost him two jobs. He is simply ___.
The brochure ___ that every room was quiet. I have my doubts.
After three complaints, the manager finally ___ that the heating was broken.
After twelve hours on the plane, I was absolutely ___.
The soup was ___ cold, so I asked them to warm it up a little.
We waited two hours for a sandwich. The service was ___ ridiculous.
___, the upgrade was free. It appeared on the bill two days later.
The hotel is small and, ___, a little old. But the staff are wonderful.
Nobody answered the door. ___, they had already left.

blocks.title: MEMORY · the neutral word and its loaded twin
blocks.intro: Find each neutral word and the critical one that states the same fact. Tap two cards.

blocks.title: ANSWER IN HER KEY
blocks.intro: Sol is in the lobby, and now she speaks to you. Every reply below is correct English. Choose the one that matches her register and her degree: no slang, no exaggeration.

lines.html: I trust the new room will be somewhat cooler.

options: Yeah, it's freezing up there. You'll love it.
Considerably cooler, I think you'll find. And the windows open.
It is the coldest room ever built in any hotel.

lines.html: And is it quiet? I don't wish to be difficult.

options: Not at all. It overlooks the courtyard, and it is almost silent.
Don't worry, you're not that difficult.
It is absolutely, totally, one hundred percent silent, I swear.

lines.html: The breakfast, I must say, was rather good.

options: Rather good? It's the best breakfast in the world!
I'm delighted to hear it. I'll pass that on to the kitchen.

lines.html: I'm afraid I was a little sharp in my note.

options: Not in the least. It was admirably clear.
Yes, it was pretty rude, to be honest.
Your note was a masterpiece of world literature.

lines.html: You have been most patient. Thank you.

options: No problem. It's my job, and I get paid for it.
It has been a pleasure. I hope the chapter goes well.
Patience is my greatest and most extraordinary quality.

blocks.title: AUDIO 2 · THE BROCHURE
blocks.desc: Julian has told Ms. Whitmore about room 412. She dictates three corrections to the brochure, changes one word at a time, and explains nothing. Explaining is your job.

questions.q: Which word does she finally choose for the view?
Why does she move from "stunning" to "partial"?
options: To make the promise match what guests really get
To make the room sound more luxurious
"Cheap" is not a real word in brochures
"Cheap" can suggest poor quality; "affordable" suggests good value

questions.q: What is wrong with "Guests have claimed that our breakfast is the best"?
options: "Claimed" makes the hotel sound as if it doubts its own guests

speaking.prompt: Explain Ms. Whitmore's three changes to a new colleague, one sentence each. Use the word 'connotation' once.
speaking.starter: She changed 'stunning' to 'partial' because… 'Cheap' became 'affordable' because… And 'claimed' became 'said' because…

transcript.html: Julian tells me the brochure needs attention. Take this down, please. The sentence about the fourth-floor rooms. As printed: "Our river rooms offer a stunning view of the water." No. "Our river rooms offer a pleasant view of the water." Hmm. Still generous. "Our river rooms offer a partial view of the water." Yes. Partial. Print that.
Now the sentence about the price. As printed: "Our rooms are cheap." Who wrote this? "Our rooms are inexpensive." Better. No. "Our rooms are affordable." That is the one.

And the last line. "Guests have claimed that our breakfast is the best in the city." Claimed! Change it. "Guests have said that our breakfast is the best in the city." Said. Thank you. Read the three sentences back to me, would you? No, never mind. I trust you. Send it to the printer.

blocks.title: <ico-pen></ico-pen> ONE ROOM, THREE VOICES
blocks.intro: The facts: a small room on the fourth floor, one window onto the street, old furniture, next to the elevator, ninety dollars a night. Describe it three times, about 40 words each: as the hotel's brochure, as an honest online review, and as a letter of complaint. The facts never change. Only the words do.
checklist: Brochure: approving words for every fact (cozy, classic, affordable, lively)
Honest review: neutral words, with at least one stance adverb (admittedly, presumably, arguably)
Complaint: critical words and one reporting verb with a verdict (claimed)
Modifiers that fit: rather / somewhat with gradable adjectives, absolutely / utterly with absolute ones
No fact added and none left out, in any version
blocks.example: BROCHURE: Our approving adjective fourth-floor rooms, with approving word for old furniture and a approving word for a street view, are price word at ninety dollars. REVIEW: The room is neutral adjective. stance adverb, one honest point. COMPLAINT: The brochure reporting verb that its promise. In fact, critical version.
blocks.hw: Write the three versions, then record yourself reading them in three different voices: the salesperson, the reviewer, the unhappy guest. Send me the text and the audio on WhatsApp.

rubric.d: Three versions of about 40 words each, with the same five facts in every one.
Each version is consistent in connotation; modifiers match their adjectives; the reporting verb and the stance adverb carry the attitude you intend.
A reader could tell which version is which with the labels removed.
